title: Salade Niçoise
subtitle: Classic Niçoise salad with tuna, eggs, and olives
excerpt: The definitive salad of Nice: tomatoes, hard-boiled eggs, black olives, anchovies, tuna, and green beans, dressed with olive oil and herbs. The authentic version never includes cooked potato or blanched vegetables, everything is fresh and raw.
sourceNotes: The salade niçoise in its authentic form is documented by Curnonsky and by the food writers of Nice as a salad of entirely raw, uncooked vegetables, tomatoes, anchovy, olive, and tuna, with hard-boiled eggs. Auguste Escoffier, who grew up near Nice, gives an early version. Elizabeth David, A Book of Mediterranean Food (1950) and French Provincial Cooking (1960), gives the canonical description and explicitly excludes cooked potato and blanched green beans, calling these 'tourist versions'. The potato version is now dominant in French bistros.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Hard-boil the eggs and prepare all the components up to 2 hours ahead. Assemble and dress just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: The French oil and vinegar dressing. The standard ratio is 3 parts oil to 1 part acid (vinegar or lemon juice). For a niçoise, olive oil is the only oil to use; wine vinegar or lemon juice is the acid.

content.text: The authentic salade niçoise has no cooked or blanched vegetables except the hard-boiled eggs. Tomatoes, raw green beans (very thinly sliced if thick, left whole if small), anchovies, black olives, and good tinned tuna, dressed with a simple olive oil
. The version with blanched green beans and cooked new potatoes is the restaurant adaptation; this recipe follows the Niçois tradition.

items.prepNote: in oil, drained and broken into chunks
very small, topped and tailed, raw

content.text: Hard-boil the eggs: lower into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes. Transfer to cold water immediately. Peel when cool and halve.
Make the vinaigrette: whisk the Dijon mustard with the red wine vinegar, then gradually whisk in the olive oil. Season with salt and pepper.

Arrange the tomato wedges on a large platter. Scatter the shallot slices over the tomatoes. Season with salt. Arrange the raw green beans, tuna chunks, egg halves, and anchovy fillets over the tomatoes. Scatter the olives and basil leaves.
Spoon the vinaigrette over the whole salad just before serving. Do not toss, salade niçoise is always presented whole and each person takes a portion from the platter.

items.symptom: The egg yolks have a grey ring
items.cause: The eggs were cooked for too long, or not transferred to cold water immediately after cooking.
items.fix: Boil for exactly 10 minutes and transfer to cold water straight away. The grey ring is ferrous sulphide formed when hydrogen sulphide in the white reacts with iron in the yolk, it only happens when the egg is overheated.

items.cause: The tomatoes were salted too far in advance, releasing their juice onto the plate.
items.fix: Salt the tomatoes immediately before adding the dressing and serving. They release liquid rapidly once salt is applied.

items.cause: The anchovies were not drained well, or the quantity was too high.
items.fix: Pat the anchovy fillets dry before using. Two per serving is the standard; the other saltier ingredients (olives, tuna in oil) are already assertive enough.

content.text: Nice and the Côte d'Azur have been making this salad since the late 19th century, when it appears in records of local café and restaurant menus. The tradition in Nice is strict about using raw vegetables only: the tomatoes must be fresh and ripe, the beans raw and thin, and the tuna should be the best available. The cooked-potato version became popular in Parisian bistros in the 20th century and spread worldwide as the better-known form. Nice does not approve of the potato.
